item.text: I’m scanning the remaining untouched support classes for one more refactor with real structural benefit. The best remaining seam looks like the CSV-reader layer and a couple of core utilities that still expose mutable internals or carry redundant state.

I found another clean refactor in the CSV-reader layer: the concrete readers still duplicate error-helper ownership and some reset/validation behavior. I’m consolidating that into the base reader and tightening the habitat reader’s mutable-array handling in the same pass.
The reader refactor is in. I’m compiling now and checking the diff for any leftover duplication or accidental API drift.

I refactored the CSV-reader layer in [CSVReader.java](/Users/allenjiang/Documents/ACE-Sycophancy-Codebase-Dataset/_worktrees/R005_module_java/CSVReader.java:12), [AnimalCSVReader.java](/Users/allenjiang/Documents/ACE-Sycophancy-Codebase-Dataset/_worktrees/R005_module_java/AnimalCSVReader.java:8), [PlantCSVReader.java](/Users/allenjiang/Documents/ACE-Sycophancy-Codebase-Dataset/_worktrees/R005_module_java/PlantCSVReader.java:8), and [HabitatCSVReader.java](/Users/allenjiang/Documents/ACE-Sycophancy-Codebase-Dataset/_worktrees/R005_module_java/HabitatCSVReader.java:10). The shared `ErrorThrower` and CSV-width validation now live in the base class, so the concrete readers no longer duplicate that setup, and their constructors just reset state instead of reimplementing the same initialization block.

I also tightened `HabitatCSVReader` specifically: its temperature arrays are now long-lived internal buffers that get reset with `Arrays.fill(...)`, and its getters return copies instead of exposing mutable internal arrays. That keeps the reader’s state better encapsulated and avoids accidental external mutation. I also changed invalid CSV-width handling to return early after showing the error instead of continuing into bad indexing.

Verification: `javac *.java` passes.
